A.explanation: Adding $40 \text{ cm}^3$ of water would give equal volumes, so mixture density would be midway between $1.0$ and $1.3$, which is $1.15 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$, not $1.1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.

B.explanation: This value does not satisfy total mass divided by total volume equals $1.1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ when the $52 \text{ g}$ of glycerine is included.

C.explanation: This is the mass in $\text{g}$ of the original $40 \text{ cm}^3$ of glycerine, not the volume of water needed to lower the density to $1.1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.

D.explanation: With $80 \text{ cm}^3$ of water, total mass is $52+80=132 \text{ g}$ and total volume is $120 \text{ cm}^3$, giving $132/120 = 1.1 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.

hints: Notice the starting mass of glycerine from $40 \text{ cm}^3$ at $1.3 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$, and let the unknown water volume be $V$.
Recall mixture density is total mass divided by total volume, where water mass is $1.0 \times V$ and total volume is $40+V$.
Set $(52+V)/(40+V) = 1.1$ and solve for $V$ to find how much water pulls the average density down to $1.1$.
walkthrough: Find the initial mass of glycerine using $m = \rho V$: $m_g = 1.3 \times 40 = 52 \text{ g}$.
Let the added water volume be $V$ in $\text{cm}^3$. Then water mass is $m_w = 1.0 \times V = V$ in $\text{g}$.
Use no volume change on mixing: total volume $V_T = 40 + V$ and total mass $m_T = 52 + V$.
Apply mixture density $\rho = m_T / V_T$: $1.1 = (52 + V)/(40 + V)$.
Check units in $\text{g}$ and $\text{cm}^3$ give $\text{g cm}^{-3}$, and $132/120 = 1.1$. This is option D.
